questions.enonce_markdown: How is the morphology and anatomy of the leaf of a maize plant adapted to photosynthesis? *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Maize is a monocotyledon and a **C$_4$ plant**. Its leaf is adapted to photosynthesis as follows.

**Morphology (external features)**

1. The blade is **long, thin and flat**, giving a **large surface area** to trap light and to take in CO$_2$; being thin, light reaches all the cells and gases diffuse over a short distance.
2. It is held **upright and arched** with the leaves spread out at different heights, so that **little shading** occurs and the leaves intercept much sunlight, even at a low angle of the sun.
3. **Parallel venation** with the veins regularly spaced, so that every photosynthetic cell is close to a vein (short distance for water, minerals and for removal of sugars).

**Anatomy (internal structure)**

4. The **epidermis is transparent**, covered by a thin **cuticle** that lets light through but reduces water loss.
5. **Stomata are present on both surfaces** (upper and lower), with guard cells controlling the entry of CO$_2$ and the loss of water vapour. **Bulliform cells** in the upper epidermis lose water and let the leaf roll up in dry conditions, reducing transpiration.
6. The **mesophyll cells** contain many **chloroplasts** with chlorophyll in grana, where the light reactions take place. There are **air spaces** between cells for the diffusion of CO$_2$ and O$_2$. The mesophyll is not divided into palisade and spongy layers.
7. **Kranz anatomy.** Each vascular bundle is surrounded by a ring of large **bundle sheath cells** containing large chloroplasts (rich in starch and with few grana), and the mesophyll cells are arranged in a ring around the sheath. CO$_2$ is first fixed in the mesophyll cells by **PEP carboxylase** (which has no affinity for O$_2$) to form oxaloacetate and then malate; the malate passes into the bundle sheath cells and releases CO$_2$ there, so that **Rubisco** works in a **high CO$_2$ concentration**. This **reduces photorespiration**, so maize photosynthesises efficiently at high temperature and light intensity.
8. **Vascular tissue:** the **xylem** brings water and minerals and the **phloem** carries away the sugars made, so that the products do not accumulate and slow down photosynthesis.

**Diagram expected.** A labelled transverse section of the maize leaf showing the upper and lower epidermis with cuticle, stomata with guard cells, bulliform cells, the vascular bundle (xylem, phloem), the ring of bundle sheath cells and the mesophyll cells around it.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms:

(i) Action spectrum. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Absorption spectrum. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Action spectrum.** A graph showing the **effectiveness (rate) of photosynthesis** (for example the rate of oxygen release or of carbon dioxide uptake) **at different wavelengths of light**. It shows which wavelengths are actually used for photosynthesis; it has two peaks, in the **blue-violet (about 450 nm)** and the **red (about 680 nm)** regions, and a trough in the green.

**(ii) Absorption spectrum.** A graph showing the **amount (percentage) of light absorbed by a pigment, or by a mixture of pigments, at different wavelengths**. Chlorophyll a absorbs mainly in the blue-violet and red regions and reflects green light; the action spectrum closely follows the combined absorption spectra of the photosynthetic pigments, which shows that these pigments are responsible for photosynthesis.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the role played by photosynthetic pigments in the light dependent phase of photosynthesis. *[8 marks]* *(8, 2, 2, 8 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The light dependent phase takes place on the **thylakoid membranes** of the chloroplast. The pigments are arranged in groups called **photosystems** (photosystem I and II), each made of a **light-harvesting (antenna) complex** and a **reaction centre**.

1. **Absorption of light.** The **accessory pigments** (chlorophyll b, carotenoids, xanthophylls) and chlorophyll a of the antenna complex **absorb light of different wavelengths**. This widens the range of wavelengths that can be used (the accessory pigments absorb wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly), so more light energy is trapped.
2. **Transfer of energy.** The light energy is passed from molecule to molecule by **resonance** to the **primary pigment**, a special chlorophyll a molecule at the **reaction centre** (**P680** in photosystem II, **P700** in photosystem I).
3. **Emission of electrons.** The reaction centre chlorophyll is **excited**: it **loses a pair of high-energy electrons**, which are taken up by an electron acceptor.
4. **Non-cyclic photophosphorylation.** Electrons from photosystem II pass along an **electron transport chain** to photosystem I. The energy released is used to pump H$^+$ into the thylakoid space; the protons flow back through **ATP synthase** (chemiosmosis), making **ATP**. The electrons lost by photosystem I are finally accepted by **NADP$^+$**, which is reduced to **NADPH** (with H$^+$).
5. **Photolysis of water.** The electrons lost by photosystem II are replaced by electrons from **water**, which is split by light: $2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- + \text{O}_2$. **Oxygen** is released as a by-product, and the H$^+$ add to the proton gradient.
6. **Cyclic photophosphorylation.** Photosystem I alone: the excited electrons return to P700 through the electron transport chain, making **ATP only** (no NADPH, no oxygen).
7. **Protection.** **Carotenoids** also protect chlorophyll from damage by excess light (photo-oxidation).

The ATP and NADPH made are used in the **light independent phase** (Calvin cycle) to reduce carbon dioxide to carbohydrate.

**Diagram expected.** The Z-scheme (energy level of electrons against the carriers: P680, acceptor, electron transport chain, P700, NADP$^+$) with labels, or a labelled drawing of a photosystem on the thylakoid membrane.
